core: Ancient art as a modern umbrella term for many historically distinct artistic practices, rather than a single style or civilization
How chronology, geography, material, use, and archaeological context guide an introductory account of an ancient work
Why comparisons should name their evidence and avoid treating one regional tradition as the default
supporting: The relationship between surviving objects, excavation context, written records, and scholarly reconstruction
The role of exchange, institutions, and patronage in some ancient artistic settings
Uncertainty in dates, names, functions, and meanings when evidence is incomplete
outOfScope: A comprehensive survey of every ancient region, dynasty, religion, or artistic medium
Detailed lessons on ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, South Asia, East Asia, Africa, the Americas, or Oceania, which require separate historical treatment
Claims about a work's market value, ownership, repatriation, authenticity, or legal status
Using ancient Greek or Roman art as a universal standard for judging other traditions

claims.claim: 'Ancient art' is a useful course label but not the name of one culture, one style, or one simultaneous global period; chronological and regional frameworks must be stated when making a comparison.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art's Heilbrunn Timeline organizes global art history through chronological, geographical, and thematic paths, making comparison possible without requiring a single linear story.
For the third-millennium Near East, the Met describes contemporary urban traditions as sharing some features of urban life while differing in their art, institutions, and cultural forms.

Archaeological and written evidence can inform accounts of ancient works, but absolute dates and original meanings may remain uncertain; a responsible account distinguishes documented evidence from inference.
A historically grounded analysis asks about a work's material, scale, production, use, setting, audience, and later survival in addition to its visible form.
The surviving material record is selective: objects from temples, tombs, palaces, elite collections, or excavated sites can be more visible than everyday or perishable practices.

conflictingEvidence.issue: A chronological label can make varied cultures look like one unified artistic world.
positions: Broad labels help students orient themselves and compare objects across time and place.
The same labels can conceal differences in language, politics, belief, material practice, chronology, and local categories.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses 'ancient art' as a navigational term only. It requires students to replace the broad label with a more precise culture, region, time range, material, and context whenever the evidence permits.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft provided no historical definition, regional scope, source-supported example, or account of how ancient material is studied.

Its vocabulary was circular, its college version was generic study-skills prose, its Eli-10 analogy had no stated limit, and its quick-check options did not meet the required four-option assessment format.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with a context-first introduction that treats ancient art as plural and historically situated.
Added a source-supported explanation of chronological uncertainty and the selectivity of surviving evidence.
Added a worked comparison method that separates observation, documentation, and cautious inference.
Rebuilt the assessment as five original four-option questions with supported keys, including application and analysis.
rightsIssues: The Met Timeline and exhibition essay are used as REFERENCE_ONLY museum scholarship; no source prose or images are reproduced.
Smarthistory is used as a REFERENCE_ONLY open educational source for its global, non-linear pedagogical framing; all prose, examples, and questions are original.

sourceRecords.title: Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History
sourceRecords.notes: Read as an authoritative museum reference. It supports the Timeline's chronological, geographical, and thematic organization of global art history and the lesson's use of multiple comparison paths rather than a single linear account. It is cited for factual framing only; no text or image is adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Art of the First Cities in the Third Millennium B.C.
sourceRecords.notes: Read as a museum essay on third-millennium B.C. Near Eastern material. It supports the distinction among contemporary urban traditions, the importance of temple, palace, and tomb contexts, and the uncertainty of early absolute chronology. The lesson does not generalize its regional claims to every ancient society.

sourceRecords.title: Reframing Art History
sourceRecords.notes: Read as a Tier B open educational overview. It supports a global art-history framing that treats regional, chronological, and methodological choices as part of interpretation. It is used for independently checked instructional framing only; all lesson prose and examples are original.
